questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{f}\colon\boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k$ with $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, what is the size of $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
What entries make up the Jacobian matrix?
Let $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,xy)$. What is $\dfrac{\partial\boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x}$?
Let $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,xy)$. What is $\dfrac{\partial\boldsymbol{f}}{\partial y}$?
How can the Jacobian be written using gradients of component functions?
options: As a single scalar sum of all gradients.
As a matrix with no relation to gradients.

questions.question: How is the total derivative related to the Jacobian matrix when $f$ is differentiable?
options: The existence of the Jacobian always implies total differentiability.
If the function is differentiable, its total derivative is equal to the Jacobian matrix.
The total derivative is unrelated to the Jacobian.
The Jacobian is defined only for scalar-valued constant functions.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,xy)$, what is $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)$?
Let $\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$ have all partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$. What size is its Jacobian at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$?
A function has all first-order partial derivatives at $x_0$, so a Jacobian matrix can be written down there. What extra conclusion is not justified from this alone?
options: That the Jacobian records first-order partial derivatives.
That the function is totally differentiable at $x_0$.
That the matrix has one row per output coordinate.
That the entries are evaluated at $x_0$.

questions.question: Why must $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ be an interior point of $\boldsymbol{E}$ for the Jacobian?
options: It makes every component function constant.
It ensures partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ are considered from within a neighbourhood in the domain.
It changes the codomain from $\mathbb{R}^k$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
It forces the Jacobian to be the zero matrix at every single interior point.

For a scalar-valued function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, how does the Jacobian relate to the gradient in the displayed definition?
options: It is the row matrix $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)^\intercal$.
It is the column matrix $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ only.
It is a $n\times n$ matrix of second derivatives.
It is the zero matrix for every scalar-valued function.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k$, what is the size of the Jacobian matrix?
What entries appear in the Jacobian matrix?
options: Partial derivatives of the component functions with respect to input variables.
Only the values of the component functions at the chosen input point.

questions.question: What does each row of $\boldsymbol{\mathrm J}\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x_0)$ represent?
options: The values of all the input variables of the function.
A finite subcover of the domain.
The transpose of the gradient of one component function $f_i$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$. What is the size of $\boldsymbol{\mathrm J}\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x_0)$?

Why is the condition that $\boldsymbol x_0$ is an interior point natural for defining the Jacobian?
options: Partial derivatives vary one coordinate in both directions near $\boldsymbol x_0$.
The Jacobian is defined only for boundary points.
Interior points make all partial derivatives automatically equal to zero.
The Jacobian needs no nearby values of the function.
